entities.name: The Sicilians
entities.body: Whose tyrants had galleys before the Persian war; whose cities Lacedaemon ordered to build five hundred ships between them and to stay neutral meanwhile; and who in the end joined the enemies of Athens against her.

entities.name: The Abderites
entities.body: Nymphodorus, whose sister married Sitalces and who brought Athens the Thracian alliance, was one of them.

entities.name: The Plataeans
entities.body: Thebes’s old enemy and Athens’s oldest ally. Three hundred Thebans came into their town in the first watch of a rainy night; they dug through their own party walls to join up unseen, barricaded the streets with wagons, drove the Thebans into the mud and the dark, and killed a hundred and eighty of them. Besieged two years later, they answered the mound with a wooden wall, tunnelled out its footings, built a crescent behind it, snapped the battering rams with beams hung on chains, and came within a wind of being burnt alive. The siege closed on four hundred of their own citizens, eighty Athenians, and a hundred and ten women to bake the bread.

entities.name: Athene
entities.body: On whose statue there were forty talents of pure gold, all of it removable — which Pericles counted among the city’s resources for a last extremity, to be used and paid back. The other deities’ temples are in the citadel with hers.

entities.name: Demeter
entities.body: Whose Eleusinian temple was one of the few places kept closed when the country population camped in the city.

entities.name: Dionysus
entities.body: Of the Marshes, in whose honour the older Dionysia are still held in Anthesterion — by the Athenians and by their Ionian descendants.

entities.name: Cleippides
entities.body: Deinias’s son, in command of the forty ships sent to catch the Mitylenians at the festival of the Malean Apollo outside the town — and, if that failed, to order them to give up their ships and pull down their walls.

entities.name: Deinias
entities.body: Cleippides’s father.

entities.name: Meleas
entities.body: A Laconian who slipped into Mitylene by galley after the first battle and advised them to send more envoys to Lacedaemon.

entities.name: Hermaeondas
entities.body: A Theban, sent with Meleas before the insurrection and unable to get there before the Athenians.

entities.name: Asopius
entities.body: Phormio’s son, whom the Acarnanians insisted on having because they would take no commander who was not some son or relative of Phormio — and who was cut off with most of his troops in the retreat from Nericus.

entities.name: Dorieus
entities.body: The Rhodian, in whose Olympiad — his second victory — the Mitylenian envoys made their case to the allies.

entities.name: Alcidas
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian high admiral, and the most cautious man in the war. He took the relief fleet to Lesbos so slowly that Mitylene had fallen seven days before he heard of it; refused Teutiaplus’s advice to fall on Paches at night, refused the Ionian exiles’ advice to raise Ionia, butchered his prisoners at Myonnesus until Samian envoys told him this was no way to free Hellas, and fled home across the open sea. At Corcyra he would not attack the town even when Brasidas urged it. He was afterwards one of the three founders of Heraclea in Trachis.

entities.name: Paches
entities.body: Epicurus’s son, who walled Mitylene in and took its surrender on terms — promising not to kill anyone until Athens had answered, and keeping it. He chased Alcidas as far as Patmos, trapped Hippias the Arcadian by a safe-conduct and shot him down inside his own fortification, and had the decree for the massacre in his hand when the second galley came into port.

entities.name: Epicurus
entities.body: Paches’s father.

entities.name: Lysicles
entities.body: One of the five commanders of the twelve ships sent to levy subsidies from the allies, who went up country from Myus across the Meander plain to the hill of Sandius and was killed there with many of his men by the Carians and the people of Anaia. Not Abronichus’s father.

entities.name: Theaenetus
entities.body: Tolmides’s son, a soothsayer, who with Eupompides thought of the escape over the Peloponnesian wall at Plataea.

entities.name: Tolmides
entities.body: Theaenetus the soothsayer’s father. Not Tolmaeus’s son.

entities.name: Eupompides
entities.body: Daimachus’s son, one of the Plataean generals and joint author of the escape.

entities.name: Daimachus
entities.body: Eupompides’s father.

entities.name: Ammias
entities.body: Coroebus’s son, first up the ladder and first on the Peloponnesian wall, at the head of twelve light-armed men with a dagger and a breastplate each.

entities.name: Coroebus
entities.body: Ammias’s father.

entities.name: Androcrates
entities.body: The hero whose chapel the escaping Plataeans kept on their right, taking the Thebes road because it was the last one the pursuers would think of.

entities.name: Salaethus
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian who got into Mitylene along a torrent bed, told them the fleet was coming, and stopped them treating with Athens — then armed the commons for a sortie, and lost the city the moment they had weapons in their hands. Found in hiding, sent to Athens and killed at once, though he offered to get the Peloponnesians away from Plataea.

entities.name: Cleomenes
entities.body: Who led the invasion of Attica in place of King Pausanias, his nephew, who was still a minor. Not the Cleomenes who drove the accursed out of Athens.

entities.name: Pausanias
entities.body: Pleistoanax’s son and king of Lacedaemon, a minor when Cleomenes invaded Attica for him. Neither the regent nor the Macedonian.

entities.name: Teutiaplus
entities.body: An Elean, who told Alcidas to sail straight for Mitylene and fall on it at night, since men who have just taken a city are as careless as any in war, and that detecting the moment when an enemy is at this disadvantage is what makes a successful general. Alcidas was not moved.

entities.name: Itamenes
entities.body: Who took the upper town of Colophon with the barbarians, having been called in by one party in a quarrel.

entities.name: Hippias
entities.body: Commander of the Arcadians in the fortified quarter at Notium, invited out to a parley by Paches on a promise of safe return, kept in custody, put back inside once the quarter had been stormed — as promised — and shot down as soon as he was in. Not the tyrant.

entities.name: Cleon
entities.body: Cleaenetus’s son, the most violent man at Athens and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons, who carried the decree to kill every adult male in Mitylene and enslave the rest, and defended it the next day: a democracy is incapable of empire, your empire is a despotism, pity and sentiment and indulgence are the three failings most fatal to it, and the penalty of rebellion must be death. He lost the second vote by a show of hands that was almost equal, and got the thousand prisoners killed instead.

snapshots.body: Cleaenetus’s son, who talked Athens out of the peace the Lacedaemonians offered for the men on the island, and then had to live with it. Accused of blocking the treaty, he called the reports from Pylos lies; offered the command of an expedition as a taunt to Nicias; found the offer taken seriously; and could not get out of his own words. He asked for no Athenian troops, promised to bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them there within twenty days, and — crazy as the promise was — kept it, having chosen Demosthenes, who had already planned the landing, as his colleague.

Cleaenetus’s son, whose luck at Pylos killed him at Amphipolis. He took Torone before Brasidas could relieve it, then sat at Eion waiting for Perdiccas and for Thracian mercenaries until his own soldiers’ contempt forced him up the road. He posted the army on a hill to look at the place, thought nobody would come out, and was sounding the retreat — wheeling his right and exposing its unarmed side — when Brasidas came out of two gates at once. He had never had any thought of fighting, fled first, and was overtaken and killed by a Myrcinian targeteer. About six hundred Athenians fell, and seven of the enemy.

entities.name: Cleaenetus
entities.body: Cleon’s father.

entities.name: Diodotus
entities.body: Eucrates’s son, who answered Cleon by refusing to argue about guilt at all: the question is not justice but the interest of Athens, and no penalty yet invented has ever stopped men from taking a risk they have set their minds on — so killing the Mitylenian commons, who had surrendered the town the moment they got arms, would only teach every future rebel to hold out to the last. His motion carried, and the second galley beat the first by the length of a meal eaten at the oar.

entities.name: Eucrates
entities.body: Diodotus’s father.

entities.name: The Mitylenians
entities.body: Who wanted to revolt before the war and were refused, and then had to do it before their walls and moles and archers were ready. They told the allies at Olympia that fear, not friendship, had kept them in the Athenian alliance, and that the liberty of attacking being always Athens’s, the liberty of defending should be theirs. Starved out, they were sentenced to death in one assembly and reprieved in the next by a handful of votes.

entities.name: The Methymnians
entities.body: The one city in Lesbos that did not revolt: they informed Athens of the preparations, fought on her side, and afterwards kept their land when the rest of the island was divided into three thousand allotments.

entities.name: The Tenedians
entities.body: At enmity with Mitylene, and among the first to tell Athens what was being prepared there.

entities.name: The Imbrians
entities.body: Who came to the aid of Athens at Mitylene with the Lemnians.

entities.name: The Lemnians
entities.body: Who came to the aid of Athens at Mitylene with the Imbrians.

entities.name: The Antissians
entities.body: Who beat the Methymnians in a sortie with their mercenaries, and were reduced by Paches afterwards.

entities.name: The Colophonians
entities.body: Whose upper town was taken by Itamenes and the barbarians in a party quarrel, and who then split again at Notium; Paches gave the place to the party that had not Medized, and Athens sent out settlers and collected the rest of them from wherever they had gone.

entities.name: Nicias
entities.body: Niceratus’s son, who took Minoa off Megara so that the blockade could be kept from a nearer station, and led sixty ships against Melos and the Locrian seaboard.

snapshots.body: Niceratus’s son, and the general Cleon taunted into losing his command at Pylos — he resigned it in the assembly and called the Athenians to witness that he had. He beat the Corinthians at Solygia, took Cythera by a mixture of battle and private correspondence, burnt Thyrea, and was wounded on the hill outside Mende; and it was to him that Perdiccas had to prove his change of side.

Niceratus’s son, the most successful general of his time and the author of the peace that carries his name. He wanted to secure his good fortune while it lasted, keep out of the way of chance, and leave behind the name of a statesman who never failed — and thought only peace made that possible. He got the treaty and then spent years watching it come apart: overlooked by Lacedaemon in favour of nobody, outmanoeuvred by Alcibiades in front of the assembly, and sent to Sparta himself to ask for Panactum standing and the Boeotian alliance given up. He came back with nothing but the oaths renewed, and was blamed for the treaty he had made.

Niceratus’s son, chosen against his will to command an expedition he had argued twice against. He told the assembly they were leaving many enemies behind to go and fetch more, and that the treaty was nominal; then, hoping to frighten them off with the size of the bill, asked for a hundred galleys and five thousand heavy infantry — and was thanked for good advice and given everything. In Sicily he sailed round the island collecting thirty talents instead of the promised fortune, argued for a show of force and a voyage home, and took the army to Syracuse only after Alcibiades had been recalled. He was in the Circle, sick, when the Syracusans came for it, and saved it by burning the engines and timber in front of the wall. The death of Lamachus left him sole commander of the siege.

entities.name: Niceratus
entities.body: Nicias’s father.

entities.name: Astymachus
entities.body: Asopolaus’s son, one of the two Plataeans deputed to answer the five Lacedaemonian judges — who put one question and no charge, and asked it again of each man before taking him out and killing him.

entities.name: Asopolaus
entities.body: Astymachus’s father.

entities.name: Lacon
entities.body: Aeimnestus’s son and proxenus of the Lacedaemonians, the other Plataean speaker.

entities.name: Aeimnestus
entities.body: Lacon’s father.

entities.name: Peithias
entities.body: A volunteer proxenus of Athens and leader of the commons at Corcyra, acquitted on a charge of enslaving the city and answering it by prosecuting five rich men for cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous. They came into the senate house with daggers and killed him and sixty others.

entities.name: Alcinous
entities.body: In whose sacred ground, with Zeus’s, the stakes were cut — a stater a stake.

entities.name: Nicostratus
entities.body: Diitrephes’s son, who came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenians and very nearly settled Corcyra: he got both parties to agree to try ten ringleaders, stopped the commons from killing men in the street, and persuaded four hundred suppliants out of the temple of Hera — and then sailed on.

entities.name: Diitrephes
entities.body: Nicostratus’s father, spelled Diotrephes at the taking of Cythera. Not the commander who leads the Thracians home in the later books.

entities.name: Eurymedon
entities.body: Thucles’s son, who came to Corcyra with sixty ships — and during the seven days he lay there the Corcyraeans went on butchering their fellow citizens, some for supposed conspiracy and some for money owed.

entities.name: Thucles
entities.body: Eurymedon’s father.

entities.name: Laches
entities.body: Melanopus’s son, who took twenty ships to Sicily with Charoeades, was left in sole command when Charoeades was killed, took Mylae and Messina, and was relieved by Pythodorus.

entities.name: Melanopus
entities.body: Laches’s father.

entities.name: Charoeades
entities.body: Euphiletus’s son, Laches’s colleague in Sicily, killed by the Syracusans in battle.

entities.name: Euphiletus
entities.body: Charoeades’s father.

entities.name: The Dioscuri
entities.body: In whose temple at Corcyra the men enrolled for the ships sat down as suppliants, fearing they were to be sent to Athens.

entities.name: The Syracusans
entities.body: At war with Leontini, with all the Dorian cities of Sicily except Camarina for allies, and blockading the Leontines by land and sea when Athens first sent ships west.

snapshots.body: Who would not believe the expedition was coming, made fun of the men who said so, and were still arguing when the fleet reached Rhegium. Beaten in the first battle by troops they outnumbered, they were told by Hermocrates that courage was not their problem and elected three generals instead of fifteen. They built counterwork after counterwork across the Athenian lines, lost each of them, and were walled in by a double wall to the sea — at which point they began to discuss terms with Nicias, deposed their generals, and blamed them for the ill fortune.

entities.name: The Leontines
entities.body: Who had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities, and who appealed to Athens on their ancient alliance and their Ionian origin.

entities.name: The Camarinaeans
entities.body: The one Dorian city of Sicily that took the Leontine side.

snapshots.body: Who heard Hermocrates and Euphemus in the same assembly and answered both alike. They liked the Athenians and had always been at enmity with Syracuse; but Syracuse was next door and might win without them, so they had already sent a few horsemen that way and meant to go on helping as sparingly as possible — and told both embassies that their oaths made it most consistent to side with neither.

entities.name: The Rhegians
entities.body: Of Italy, who were for their Leontine kinsmen, and whose town the Athenians made their base.

snapshots.body: Chalcidians and kinsmen of the Leontines, and the people Athens had most reason to count on. They would not take the armament inside their walls, gave it a market outside the city in the precinct of Artemis, and said they would side with neither party but wait and do whatever the rest of the Italiots did.

entities.name: The Locrians of Italy
entities.body: Who were for the Syracusans, beat the Athenians at their fort on the Halex and again under Pythodorus, and were beaten on the Caicinus. Not the Ozolian or Opuntian Locrians of Greece.

entities.name: Agis
entities.body: Archidamus’s son, who brought the army as far as the Isthmus and turned back without invading because of the earthquakes.

snapshots.body: Archidamus’s son, king of Lacedaemon, who nearly lost the Peloponnese and then saved it in an afternoon. He had the Argives surrounded before their own walls and granted them a four-month truce instead, on the word of two men who had no authority to give it — for which Sparta came within a vote of razing his house and fining him ten thousand drachmae, and did pass a law attaching ten counsellors to him without whose consent he could not lead an army out. At Mantinea he ordered his left extended in the moment of the onset, two polemarchs refused to fill the gap, and the Mantineans poured through it; he turned the whole army on the broken wing and won the greatest Hellenic battle for a very long time.

entities.name: Demosthenes
entities.body: Alcisthenes’s son. Talked by the Messenians into invading Aetolia against the Acarnanians’ advice, he pushed on without waiting for his Locrian darters, lost his archers’ captain and then his guide, and watched a hundred and twenty Athenian hoplites — by far the best men of the city to fall in the war — die in trackless gullies and in a wood the Aetolians burned around them. He stayed at Naupactus afraid to face Athens; and then saved Naupactus, hid four hundred men in a hollow road at Olpae, broke Eurylochus’s wing from behind, and destroyed the Ambraciot relief at Idomene at dawn by putting Messenians in front to speak Doric to the sentries.

snapshots.body: Alcisthenes’s son, who asked for nothing but leave to use the fleet on the Peloponnesian coast, was carried into Pylos by a squall, and could not persuade the generals or the soldiers to fortify it — until the soldiers, with no iron tools, did it themselves in six days with stones that happened to fit and mortar carried on their backs. He was left with five ships, armed his sailors with osier shields off a Messenian privateer, and held the one landing place he had judged the enemy would choose. Afterwards, with the island burnt bare by an accidental fire, he planned the descent that surrounded four hundred and twenty Lacedaemonians with light troops who could conquer in flight, and would not let the killing finish.

entities.name: Alcisthenes
entities.body: Demosthenes’s father.

entities.name: Procles
entities.body: Theodorus’s son, Demosthenes’s colleague in the thirty ships, and among the slain in Aetolia.

entities.name: Theodorus
entities.body: Procles’s father.

entities.name: Hipponicus
entities.body: Callias’s son, who brought the whole levy from Athens to meet the fleet at Tanagra by prearranged signal.

entities.name: Callias
entities.body: Hipponicus’s father. Neither the Corinthian admiral’s father nor the Athenian general killed at Potidaea.

entities.name: Tisamenus
entities.body: The ambassador the Trachinians chose to ask Lacedaemon for a colony, after suffering severely in a war with the Oetaeans.

entities.name: Leon
entities.body: One of the three Lacedaemonians who led out the colony to Heraclea in Trachis.

entities.name: Damagon
entities.body: The third founder of Heraclea, with Leon and Alcidas.

entities.name: Hesiod
entities.body: The poet, said to have been killed by the people of the country in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, in fulfilment of an oracle that he would die at Nemea — where Demosthenes’s army bivouacked on its way into Aetolia.

entities.name: Chromon
entities.body: The Messenian who guided the army in Aetolia, and whose death left it in trackless country.

entities.name: Tolophus
entities.body: An Ophionian, one of the three Aetolian envoys who got an army out of Corinth and Lacedaemon against Naupactus.

entities.name: Boriades
entities.body: A Eurytanian, the second of the three Aetolian envoys.

entities.name: Tisander
entities.body: An Apodotian, the third of the three Aetolian envoys.

entities.name: Eurylochus
entities.body: The Spartan who brought three thousand heavy infantry against Naupactus, took hostages from most of Ozolian Locris on the way, missed the town by a thousand men Demosthenes had got in, and then waited in Aetolia for the Ambraciots. At Olpae his own wing and his best troops were broken from behind by men out of a hollow road, and he was killed with them.

entities.name: Macarius
entities.body: A Spartan, one of Eurylochus’s two colleagues, and killed with him at Olpae.

entities.name: Menedaius
entities.body: The surviving Spartan commander at Olpae, who could neither stand a siege nor retreat, asked for a truce to take up the dead — and was quietly given leave to slip away with the Mantineans and the other leaders, which is exactly what Demosthenes wanted the Hellenes of those parts to hear about.

entities.name: Proxenus
entities.body: Capaton’s son, who led the Italian Locrians against the Athenians on the river Caicinus.

entities.name: Capaton
entities.body: Proxenus’s father.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: Timocrates’s son, one of the two commanders of the twenty Athenian ships the Acarnanians sent for.

entities.name: Timocrates
entities.body: Aristotle the commander’s father. Neither Timoxenus’s father nor the Lacedaemonian who killed himself off Naupactus.

entities.name: Hierophon
entities.body: Antimnestus’s son, the other commander of the twenty ships.

entities.name: Antimnestus
entities.body: Hierophon’s father.

entities.name: Salynthius
entities.body: The friendly king of the Agraeans, with whom the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who got away from Olpae took refuge.

entities.name: Pythodorus
entities.body: Isolochus’s son, sent out to relieve Laches in Sicily, and beaten by the Locrians at the fort Laches had taken. Not the archon of the year the war began.

entities.name: Isolochus
entities.body: Pythodorus the general’s father.

entities.name: Sophocles
entities.body: Sostratides’s son, who was to follow Pythodorus to Sicily with the main body.

entities.name: Sostratides
entities.body: Sophocles’s father.

entities.name: Hephaestus
entities.body: Whose forge the people of those parts believe to be on Hiera, from the flame the island sends out by night and the smoke by day.

entities.name: The Melians
entities.body: Islanders who refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy, and whose land was devastated without bringing them to terms.

snapshots.body: A colony of Lacedaemon that would not be subjects like the other islanders. Told by the Athenian envoys that right is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must, they answered that they would not in a moment give up the freedom of a city seven hundred years old, and trusted to fortune, to the gods, and to the Lacedaemonians. They broke the lines twice by night. Then treachery inside ended it: the Athenians killed all the grown men they took, sold the women and children, and sent out five hundred colonists of their own.

entities.name: The Malians
entities.body: Three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans and the Trachinians.

entities.name: The Paralians
entities.body: One of the three Malian tribes.

entities.name: The Hiereans
entities.body: One of the three Malian tribes.

entities.name: The Trachinians
entities.body: The Malian tribe that had suffered severely from the Oetaeans, thought of putting themselves under Athens, and asked Lacedaemon for a colony instead — which became Heraclea, and which the Thessalians and Lacedaemon’s own governors between them wore down.

entities.name: The Oetaeans
entities.body: The neighbours whose war on the Trachinians brought Heraclea into existence.

entities.name: The Apodotians
entities.body: The Aetolian tribe the Messenians told Demosthenes to attack first.

entities.name: The Ophionians
entities.body: The Aetolian tribe to be attacked second; the most remote of them, the Bomiensians and Calliensians, came down to the rescue with the rest.

entities.name: The Eurytanians
entities.body: The largest tribe in Aetolia, who speak, it is said, an extremely difficult language and eat their flesh raw.

entities.name: The Bomiensians
entities.body: The most remote of the Ophionians, who extend toward the Malian gulf.

entities.name: The Calliensians
entities.body: The other remote Ophionian tribe, who came down against Demosthenes with the rest.

entities.name: The Amphissians
entities.body: Eurylochus’s chief supporters in Ozolian Locris, alarmed at the hostility of the Phocians, who gave hostages first and talked the rest into it.

entities.name: The Myonians
entities.body: Who held the most difficult of the passes into Locris, and gave hostages after the Amphissians.

entities.name: The Ipnians
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Messapians
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Tritaeans
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Chalaeans
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Tolophonians
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Hessians
entities.body: One of the Ozolian Locrian towns that gave hostages and joined the expedition.

entities.name: The Oeanthians
entities.body: The last of the Ozolian Locrian towns to give hostages and join the expedition.

entities.name: The Olpaeans
entities.body: Who gave hostages but would not join the invasion.

entities.name: The Hyaeans
entities.body: Who would do neither, until Eurylochus took one of their villages.

entities.name: The Mantineans
entities.body: Massed on the left at Olpae, and the only unit that kept its ranks in the retreat — which is why Demosthenes and the Acarnanians quietly let them go, to discredit the Lacedaemonians with the Hellenes of those parts as traitors and self-seekers.

snapshots.body: Who had used the Attic war to bring much of Arcadia under them and went over to Argos for fear Lacedaemon would take it back. They held the right at the battle fought in their own country, broke the Sciritae and Brasideans and poured into the gap Agis had opened, and then had to run when the rest of the line collapsed behind them. When Argos changed sides they found they could do nothing alone, came to terms, and gave up their sovereignty over the towns.

entities.name: The Liparaeans
entities.body: A Cnidian colony holding the islands of Aeolus from Lipara, and allies of Syracuse.

entities.name: The Sicels
entities.body: Some of them subjects or allies of Syracuse and some in revolt from her; they invaded Himera from the interior while the Athenians landed on the coast.

snapshots.body: Who came over to the Athenians once there was something to come over to. Those in the lowlands and subject to Syracuse mostly held aloof; the peoples of the interior, who had never been anything but independent, joined almost at once and brought down corn and sometimes money — and more of them came when the double wall began to reach the sea.

entities.name: The Catanians
entities.body: Who live on Etna, the largest mountain in Sicily, and lost some of their land to the stream of fire.

entities.name: The Cephallenians
entities.body: Whose four states — Pale, Crane, Same and Pronae — came over to Athens without force, and who joined the levy against Leucas and went with Demosthenes into Aetolia.

entities.name: Epitadas
entities.body: Molobrus’s son, who commanded the four hundred and twenty heavy infantry drafted by lot onto Sphacteria. He kept them on half rations while Helots ran corn and wine in by night for the promise of freedom, held the level middle of the island where the water was, closed ranks when the outpost was cut off, and could neither reach the light troops nor be let alone by them. He was killed before the surrender.

entities.name: Molobrus
entities.body: Epitadas’s father.

entities.name: Thrasymelidas
entities.body: Cratesicles’s son, a Spartan, and admiral of the forty-three ships that attacked the new fort from the sea at exactly the point Demosthenes had expected.

entities.name: Cratesicles
entities.body: Thrasymelidas’s father.

entities.name: Simonides
entities.body: The Athenian general who gathered a few men from the garrisons and some allies of those parts and took Eion in Thrace by treachery — and was beaten out of it again by the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans with the loss of many of his soldiers.

entities.name: Demoteles
entities.body: Who commanded the garrison left in Messina after the disaster at Naxos, and led the sally that broke most of the Leontine army.

entities.name: Archias
entities.body: Whose party was about to betray Camarina to Syracuse when the Athenians got warning and sailed there. Not the Corinthian who founded Syracuse.

entities.name: Styphon
entities.body: Pharax’s son, and third in the Spartan line of command on the island: Epitadas was dead and Hippagretas left for dead among the slain, so by law it fell to him. He asked the mainland what to do, and after the question had gone back and forth two or three times was told to decide for himself, so long as he did nothing dishonourable.

entities.name: Pharax
entities.body: Styphon’s father.

entities.name: Hippagretas
entities.body: The Spartan next in command after Epitadas, left for dead among the slain and still alive.

entities.name: Theagenes
entities.body: Chosen with Cleon to go and see for himself whether the reports from Pylos were true — a commission Cleon talked the assembly out of before it could sail. Not the tyrant of Megara.

entities.name: Ulysses
entities.body: Whom the story makes sail through the Charybdis: the strait between Rhegium and Messina, where Sicily comes nearest the continent, and where the current out of the Tyrrhenian and Sicilian mains has rightly given the narrows a bad name.

entities.name: The Messinese
entities.body: The people of Messina in Sicily, who let in the Syracusan and Locrian ships and revolted from Athens, then attacked Chalcidian Naxos and lost more than a thousand men to a sally and most of the rest to the barbarians on the road home — and who still had a sally left in them that broke the Leontine army.

entities.name: The Naxians
entities.body: The Chalcidian people of Naxos in Sicily, kept inside their walls on the first day and out of their gates on the second: they saw the Sicels coming down from the high country, believed the Leontines were coming too, and routed the Messinese.

entities.name: Battus
entities.body: One of the two Corinthian generals at Solygia, who took a company to hold the unwalled village while Lycophron gave battle with the rest.

entities.name: Lycophron
entities.body: The Corinthian general at Solygia, who held the right wing against the Athenian left for a long time and was among the dead when the Athenian cavalry — the Corinthians had none — finally turned it. Not the Lacedaemonian commissioner sent to Cnemus.

entities.name: Aristides
entities.body: Archippus’s son, one of the commanders of the squadron sent round to collect money from the allies. He arrested Artaphernes at Eion with the King’s dispatches on him, and afterwards helped Demodocus retake Antandrus from the Mitylenian exiles. Not Lysimachus’s son.

entities.name: Archippus
entities.body: Aristides the commander’s father.

entities.name: Artaphernes
entities.body: The Persian taken at Eion on his way from the King to Lacedaemon. His dispatches, translated at Athens out of the Assyrian script, said that the King could not make out what the Lacedaemonians wanted, since of the many ambassadors they had sent him no two ever told the same story: let them send plain men with this Persian and say so. The Athenians sent him back to Ephesus with envoys of their own.

entities.name: Hermocrates
entities.body: Hermon’s son, a Syracusan, and the most influential man at the congress of Gela. He told the Sicilians that the question before them was not their several grievances but whether there was still time to save the island; that no one should think the Dorians alone were the enemy while Chalcidian blood protected the rest, since the attack was aimed not at a nationality but at what was in Sicily, the common property of them all; and that the quickest way to be rid of the guests was to stop giving them a reason to stay. They took his advice and kept what they had.

snapshots.body: Hermon’s son, who told an assembly that would not believe him that the Athenians were already on the voyage, and that the way to stop them was to meet them at Tarentum before they ever reached Sicily. After the first defeat he told the Syracusans that their spirit had not been beaten, only their discipline — fifteen generals and too many orders — and had them elect three with full powers and an oath to leave them alone; he was one. It was his idea to stop fighting pitched battles and build counterworks across the line the Athenian wall had to take.

entities.name: Hermon
entities.body: Hermocrates’s father.

entities.name: Autocles
entities.body: Tolmaeus’s son, third in the command that took Cythera, and one of the three Athenian generals who swore to the year’s armistice.

entities.name: Tolmaeus
entities.body: Autocles’s father. The history never says whether he is the Tolmaeus whose son Tolmides sailed round the Peloponnese.

entities.name: Tantalus
entities.body: Patrocles’s son, the Lacedaemonian commanding at Thyrea, wounded and taken alive when the Athenians burnt the town, and sent to share the imprisonment of the men from the island.

entities.name: Patrocles
entities.body: Tantalus’s father.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: Ariphron’s son. With Demosthenes he took the long walls of Megara by an ambush at a gate that was opened every night for a smuggler’s boat on a cart; and then designed the double stroke on Boeotia — Siphae and Chaeronea handed over on an appointed day while he fortified Delium, so that the Boeotians could not unite against any of it. The days were mistaken and the plot was betrayed, and he was left to fortify the sanctuary of Apollo alone and to fight Pagondas with a mass levy that had mostly gone home. He fell in the rout with nearly a thousand Athenians. Not the Lacedaemonian of the later books.

entities.name: Ariphron
entities.body: Hippocrates the general’s father.

entities.name: Enyalius
entities.body: In whose precinct, nearer Megara than the quarry, Demosthenes lay in ambush with the Plataean light troops and the Peripoli.

entities.name: The Andrians
entities.body: Whose contingent served under Nicias against Corinth; and whose colonies — Acanthus, Stagirus, Argilus, Sane — stand in the Thracian country Brasidas was about to walk through.

entities.name: The Carystians
entities.body: Placed at the end of the Athenian line at Solygia, where with the Athenian right they took the first Corinthian charge, gave ground, and twice drove it back.

entities.name: The Cytherians
entities.body: Lacedaemonians of the Perioeci class, on the island that took the merchantmen from Egypt and Libya and kept privateers off the one assailable stretch of the Laconian coast. A judge went over to them from Sparta every year. They held their ground a little while, capitulated to Nicias — with whom some of them had been in correspondence — and kept their lands at four talents tribute.

entities.name: The Peripoli
entities.body: The Athenian frontier patrol, who ran in at the Megarian gates with Demosthenes and the Plataeans, just where the trophy now stands.

entities.name: Demodocus
entities.body: One of the two commanders of the Athenian money-collecting squadron, who heard on the Hellespont what was being done at Antandrus and retook the place before it could become a second Anaia.

entities.name: Lamachus
entities.body: Their third colleague, who took ten ships into the Pontus and lost them at anchor in the Calex when rain inland brought a flood down on them, and marched his men overland through the Bithynian Thracians to Chalcedon.

snapshots.body: Xenophanes’s son, the third general, who wanted to sail straight for Syracuse and fight under the walls while the panic was at its height, since every armament is most terrible at first. He was overruled, and supported Alcibiades. Going to the help of a broken Athenian tribe at the counterwall, he crossed a ditch with a few men, was cut off on the far side, and was killed with five or six of them; the Syracusans carried the bodies off and gave them back under truce.

entities.name: Ptoeodorus
entities.body: A Theban exile, and the chief mover in the plot to change the constitutions of the Boeotian cities and bring in democracy as at Athens.

entities.name: Panaerus
entities.body: One of the Thessalians who came to Melitia to escort Brasidas through a country whose people had always sympathised with Athens — and which, Thucydides says, he could never have crossed at all if it had not been governed by a close oligarchy.

entities.name: Dorus
entities.body: One of Brasidas’s Thessalian escort.

entities.name: Hippolochidas
entities.body: One of Brasidas’s Thessalian escort.

entities.name: Torylaus
entities.body: One of Brasidas’s Thessalian escort.

entities.name: Strophacus
entities.body: The Chalcidian proxenus among Brasidas’s Thessalian escort.

entities.name: Niconidas
entities.body: Of Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas, and one of the other Thessalians who went along.

entities.name: Arrhabaeus
entities.body: Bromerus’s son and king of the Lyncestian Macedonians — the neighbour Perdiccas most wanted put down, and the reason he had paid for a Peloponnesian army. Brasidas parleyed with him instead of invading, and Perdiccas cut his contribution from half the army’s keep to a third. On the second expedition the Lyncestians were beaten in the field and took to the heights; then the Illyrian mercenaries hired for Perdiccas came over to Arrhabaeus instead, and it was the Peloponnesians who had to fight their way home.

entities.name: Bromerus
entities.body: Arrhabaeus’s father.

entities.name: Nicomachus
entities.body: A Phocian of Phanotis, who betrayed the plot on Siphae and Chaeronea to the Lacedaemonians, and they to the Boeotians.

entities.name: Pagondas
entities.body: Aeolidas’s son, Boeotarch of Thebes and commander-in-chief at Delium, and the one of the eleven who wanted to fight after the Athenians had already crossed back over the border. He told them that with a neighbour like this there is no frontier to argue about, since conquest would mean one frontier for the whole country; massed the Thebans twenty-five shields deep on the right; and when his left was breaking sent two squadrons of horse round the hill where they could not be seen, whose sudden appearance panicked the winning Athenian wing into thinking a second army had come.

entities.name: Aeolidas
entities.body: Pagondas’s father.

entities.name: Arianthides
entities.body: Lysimachidas’s son, and the other Boeotarch of Thebes.

entities.name: Lysimachidas
entities.body: Arianthides’s father.

entities.name: Aristagoras
entities.body: The Milesian who first tried to settle the spot that became Amphipolis, when he fled from King Darius, and was dislodged by the Edonians.

entities.name: Eucles
entities.body: The general sent from Athens to defend Amphipolis. He could not get the gates held, sent down the coast for Thucydides, and watched the town accept Brasidas’s terms while the citizens stopped listening to him.

entities.name: Olorus
entities.body: Thucydides’s father.

entities.name: Pittacus
entities.body: King of the Edonians, killed by the sons of Goaxis and by his own wife Brauro — after which his town of Myrcinus came over to Brasidas.

entities.name: Goaxis
entities.body: Whose sons killed the Edonian king.

entities.name: Brauro
entities.body: Pittacus’s wife, and one of his killers.

entities.name: Lysistratus
entities.body: An Olynthian, who commanded the seven light-armed men with daggers — the only ones of twenty ordered on the service who dared go in — that passed through the sea wall at Torone and cut down the guard of the highest post in the town.

entities.name: Phoenippus
entities.body: Secretary when the Athenians voted the year’s armistice.

entities.name: Niciades
entities.body: Chairman when the Athenians voted the year’s armistice.

entities.name: Taurus
entities.body: Echetimides’s son, one of the three Lacedaemonians who concluded the armistice and poured the libation.

entities.name: Echetimides
entities.body: Taurus’s father.

entities.name: Athenaeus
entities.body: Pericleidas’s son, a Lacedaemonian signatory to the armistice, and the commissioner who carried it round to Brasidas in Thrace.

entities.name: Pericleidas
entities.body: Athenaeus’s father.

entities.name: Philocharidas
entities.body: Eryxidaidas’s son, the third of the Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Eryxidaidas
entities.body: Philocharidas’s father.

entities.name: Aeneas
entities.body: Ocytus’s son, one of the two Corinthian signatories.

entities.name: Ocytus
entities.body: Aeneas’s father.

entities.name: Damotimus
entities.body: Naucrates’s son, one of the two Sicyonian signatories.

entities.name: Naucrates
entities.body: Damotimus’s father.

entities.name: Onasimus
entities.body: Megacles’s son, the other Sicyonian signatory.

entities.name: Megacles
entities.body: Onasimus’s father.

entities.name: Nicasus
entities.body: Cecalus’s son, one of the two Megarian signatories.

entities.name: Cecalus
entities.body: Nicasus’s father.

entities.name: Menecrates
entities.body: Amphidorus’s son, the other Megarian signatory.

entities.name: Amphidorus
entities.body: Menecrates’s father.

entities.name: Amphias
entities.body: Eupaidas’s son, an Epidaurian, and the last of the signatories before the three Athenian generals.

entities.name: Eupaidas
entities.body: Amphias’s father.

entities.name: Aristonymus
entities.body: The Athenian commissioner who carried the armistice round the Thracian towns. He made no difficulty about the rest, but counted the days, found that Scione had gone over after the convention, and refused to include it — on which Brasidas said flatly that the revolt had come first and would not give the town up. The facts were rather as the Athenians contended. Not Euphamidas’s father.

entities.name: Polydamidas
entities.body: The commander Brasidas sent over to Scione and Mende with five hundred Peloponnesian heavy infantry and three hundred Chalcidian targeteers. Inside Mende he drew up the piled arms for a sortie, was answered factiously by one of the popular party, and dragged the man by the arm and knocked him about — which put the commons into their arms and lost him the town in an afternoon.

entities.name: Ischagoras
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian whose overland army for Brasidas was stopped before it started, by Perdiccas setting his friends in Thessaly in motion. He got through himself with Ameinias and Aristeus to see how matters stood, and brought out from Sparta — in violation of all precedent — young men to be put in command of the towns, rather than leave them to persons on the spot.

entities.name: Ameinias
entities.body: One of the two who reached Brasidas with Ischagoras.

entities.name: Aristeus
entities.body: The third of the Lacedaemonians who reached Brasidas to inspect the state of affairs. Neither of the two Corinthians of that name.

entities.name: Clearidas
entities.body: Cleonymus’s son, one of the young Spartans brought out against precedent to command the towns, and placed by Brasidas in Amphipolis.

snapshots.body: Cleonymus’s son, left in command at Amphipolis with the bulk of the force, who came out of the Thracian gates on Brasidas’s signal and finished the battle after Brasidas fell. Ordered by the peace to hand the town over to Athens, he would not — obliging the Chalcidians, and pleading that he could not do it against their will — and went to Lacedaemon in person to see whether the agreement could still be changed. It could not, and he was sent back to hand it over if he could and in any case to bring the Peloponnesians out.

entities.name: Cleonymus
entities.body: Clearidas’s father.

entities.name: Pasitelidas
entities.body: Hegesander’s son, the other of the young Spartans, and placed in Torone.

entities.name: Hegesander
entities.body: Pasitelidas’s father.

entities.name: Phaeinis
entities.body: The priestess the Argives appointed in Chrysis’s place, agreeably to the law in such a case, after the temple of Hera burned.

entities.name: Nisus
entities.body: Whose temple at Nisaea marks one end of the road that the armistice forbade either side to cross.

entities.name: The Acanthians
entities.body: Divided over whether to admit Brasidas, they let him in alone to speak and then voted in secret — swayed, Thucydides says, as much by fear for a vintage still out on the vines as by his seductive arguments. They would not admit the army until he had given his personal security for the oaths sworn at home.

entities.name: The Toronaeans
entities.body: Whose few partisans broke down the postern from within, cut through the bar of the market gates, and let the targeteers in; and whose other party fled to Lecythus with the Athenians and were invited home again without fear for their rights or persons.

entities.name: The Scionaeans
entities.body: Who say they are Pallenians from the Peloponnese, carried in to the spot by the storm that caught the Achaeans on the voyage from Troy. They revolted while the armistice was being carried round, crowned Brasidas with a crown of gold as the liberator of Hellas and garlanded him privately like an athlete — and had a decree passed at Athens, on Cleon’s motion, to reduce them and put them to death.

snapshots.body: Who had crowned Brasidas as the liberator of Hellas. Athens reduced the town, put the adult males to death, made slaves of the women and children, and gave the land to the Plataeans to live in.

entities.name: The Mendaeans
entities.body: An Eretrian colony in Pallene, brought over by a few conspirators who had carried on their practices too long not to fear detection; and the commons who turned on Polydamidas, let the Athenians in without any convention, and were told afterwards that they might keep their civil rights and judge the authors of the revolt themselves.

entities.name: The Perrhaebians
entities.body: Subjects of Thessaly, who took Brasidas on from the border and set him down at Dium in Perdiccas’s country, under Mount Olympus.

entities.name: The Thespians
entities.body: Who stood where the Boeotian left was worsted at Delium, and when the troops beside them gave way were surrounded in a narrow space and cut down fighting hand to hand. That same summer the Thebans pulled down their wall on the charge of Atticism, having always wished to, and finding it easy now that the flower of the Thespian youth was gone.

entities.name: The Orchomenians
entities.body: Of the Boeotian Orchomenus — formerly the Minyan — on the left at Delium. Not the Arcadians of the same name.

entities.name: The Haliartians
entities.body: One of the peoples about the lake, in the Boeotian centre at Delium.

entities.name: The Coronaeans
entities.body: One of the peoples about the lake, in the Boeotian centre at Delium.

entities.name: The Copaeans
entities.body: One of the peoples about the lake, in the Boeotian centre at Delium.

entities.name: The Bisaltians
entities.body: One of the stocks in the small mixed towns of Acte, under Athos, where two languages are spoken.

entities.name: The Crestonians
entities.body: Another of the stocks in the small towns of Acte.

entities.name: The Methonaeans
entities.body: A hundred and twenty of their light-armed went up the path outside Mende with Nicias and the archers.

entities.name: The Amphipolitans
entities.body: Who had houses all over the quarter outside the wall, and of whom only a small number were Athenians — which is why Brasidas’s moderate proclamation looked fair to them compared with what their fear had suggested.

entities.name: The Pallenians
entities.body: From the Peloponnese, whom the Scionaeans claim as their first founders.

entities.name: The Euboeans
entities.body: At whose condition, and at most of the rest of Hellas, Pagondas told the Boeotians to look and be convinced.

entities.name: Acamantis
entities.body: The Athenian tribe that held the prytany when the armistice was voted.

entities.name: The Chalcidian Race
entities.body: Chalcidians out of Euboea and the cities they made in Sicily — Naxos first, then Leontini, Catana, Zancle and Himera — Ionian by blood, which Hermocrates told the congress at Gela would not save them, since the attack was not inspired by hatred of one of two nationalities but by a desire for the good things in Sicily. He said the same thing at Camarina from the other side: Athens cherishes the Chalcidians of Leontini and keeps the Chalcidians of Euboea in servitude. Not the Chalcidians of the Thracian seaboard.

entities.name: Phaeax
entities.body: Erasistratus’s son, sent with two colleagues to Italy and Sicily to talk the Sicilians into a general coalition against Syracuse and so save the commons of Leontini. He succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, was rebuffed at Gela, and gave the rest up rather than be refused again; on the way home he made terms with the Locrian settlers he met, who were the only allies that had not come into the Sicilian peace.

entities.name: Erasistratus
entities.body: Phaeax’s father.

entities.name: Polles
entities.body: King of the Odomantians, whom Cleon asked for as many Thracian mercenaries as he could bring. Cleon was still waiting for them at Eion when his own soldiers’ grumbling forced him up to Amphipolis.

entities.name: Autocharidas
entities.body: One of the three Lacedaemonians who took nine hundred heavy infantry toward Thrace, got as far as Pierium in Thessaly, and turned back when they heard Brasidas was dead.

entities.name: Epicydidas
entities.body: The third of them.

entities.name: Aristocles
entities.body: Pleistoanax’s brother, accused with him of bribing the prophetess at Delphi to tell every Lacedaemonian deputation that arrived to bring home the seed of the demigod son of Zeus, or else plough with a silver ploughshare. Not the polemarch who would not move his company at Mantinea.

entities.name: Pleistolas
entities.body: The ephor at Lacedaemon by whose year the Peace of Nicias is dated, and one of the seventeen who swore to it.

entities.name: Alcaeus
entities.body: The archon at Athens by whose year the peace is dated.

entities.name: Damagetus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonians who swore to the peace and to the alliance. The two lists spell him Damagetis and Damagetus.

entities.name: Chionis
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Metagenes
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Acanthus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories, who shares his name with the Andrian colony Brasidas talked into revolt.

entities.name: Daithus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Zeuxidas
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Antippus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Alcinadas
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Empedias
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Menas
entities.body: A Lacedaemonian signatory, and one of the three envoys sent to Thrace with orders to Clearidas to hand Amphipolis over — which he did not.

entities.name: Laphilus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories.

entities.name: Tellis
entities.body: One of the seventeen Lacedaemonian signatories. He is given no patronymic and the history does not say whether he is Brasidas’s father.

entities.name: Lampon
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenians who swore to the peace and to the alliance, and first on both lists.

entities.name: Isthmonicus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. The two lists spell him Isthmonicus and Isthmionicus.

entities.name: Euthydemus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. He is given no patronymic and the history does not say whether he is the Euthydemus who commanded in Sicily.

entities.name: Procles
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. Not Theodorus’s son, who was killed in Aetolia.

entities.name: Pythodorus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. He is given no patronymic, and the history does not say which of the two Pythodoruses it is.

entities.name: Myrtilus
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories.

entities.name: Thrasycles
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. He is given no patronymic and the history does not say whether he is the commander of Book 8.

entities.name: Aristocrates
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. He is given no patronymic and the history does not say whether he is either of the later Aristocrateses.

entities.name: Iolcius
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories.

entities.name: Timocrates
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories. Neither the Corinthian, the Lacedaemonian who killed himself off Naupactus, nor Aristotle’s father.

entities.name: Leon
entities.body: One of the seventeen Athenian signatories.

entities.name: Ampelidas
entities.body: One of the two Lacedaemonians whose application to renew the thirty years’ truce Argos refused, which is what made Lacedaemon turn to the Athenian alliance instead.

entities.name: Lichas
entities.body: Arcesilaus’s son, a Lacedaemonian, and Argos’s proxenus at Sparta. He was scourged on the course at Olympia by the umpires for coming forward and crowning his own charioteer after his horses had been proclaimed a Boeotian victory — Lacedaemon being excluded from the games that year — and afterwards carried to Argos the two proposals, war or peace, that broke the Argive league.

entities.name: Arcesilaus
entities.body: Lichas’s father.

entities.name: Pharnaces
entities.body: Who gave the Delians Atramyttium in Asia to live in when Athens expelled them from their island. The history does not say whether he is the Pharnaces whose son Artabazus carried Pausanias’s letters.

entities.name: The Delians
entities.body: Expelled from their own island by Athens, which had concluded that some old offence at the time of their consecration was the flaw in the purification; they were given Atramyttium in Asia by Pharnaces, and brought back two years later on the command of the god at Delphi.

entities.name: The Olynthians
entities.body: With whom the Athenians exchanged the prisoners from Torone, and who took Mecyberna and its Athenian garrison during the peace.

entities.name: The Hipponians
entities.body: Colonists of the Locrians of Italy, and at war with them on their border — which is why the Locrians came into the treaty with Athens at last.

entities.name: The Medmaeans
entities.body: The other Locrian colony at war with its mother city.

entities.name: The Mecybernaeans
entities.body: One of the three Chalcidian peoples the peace left in their own cities.

entities.name: The Sanaeans
entities.body: One of the three.

entities.name: The Singaeans
entities.body: The third.

entities.name: The Myrcinians
entities.body: Of the Edonian town that came over to Brasidas. One of their targeteers overtook and killed Cleon; their horse and the Chalcidians’ finished the Athenian right.

entities.name: Alcibiades
entities.body: Clinias’s son, still young for high office in any other Hellenic city but distinguished by the splendour of his ancestry — and offended that Lacedaemon had made the peace through Nicias and Laches and passed him over. He sent privately to Argos to bring the Argives, Mantineans and Eleans to Athens; trapped the Lacedaemonian envoys into denying in the assembly the full powers they had claimed in the senate, by promising privately to give Pylos back for them; and carried the hundred years’ alliance. Afterwards he marched about the Peloponnese settling the league’s affairs, had the Athenians write on the Laconian pillar that Lacedaemon had not kept her oaths, and when Argos went over at last carried off three hundred suspected men and lodged them in the islands.

snapshots.body: Clinias’s son, who talked Athens into Sicily and then talked Sparta into Decelea. He answered Nicias with his seven chariots at Olympia and the argument that a city not inactive by nature ruins itself fastest by suddenly becoming so — and that an empire cannot fix the point at which it stops. Recalled on the charge of profaning the Mysteries, he sailed as far as Thurii with the Salaminia and disappeared; sentenced to death in absence, he crossed to the Peloponnese and was invited to Lacedaemon. There he set out the whole plan of the expedition — Sicily, then Italy, then Carthage, then the Peloponnese — asked for a Spartan commander for Syracuse and a fort at Decelea, and told them that love of country is not what a man feels when he is wronged.

entities.name: Clinias
entities.body: Alcibiades’s father. Not Cleopompus’s father.

entities.name: Cleobulus
entities.body: One of the two ephors most anxious to break the treaty off, who took the Boeotians and Corinthians aside and told them to get themselves into alliance with Argos first and with Lacedaemon afterwards.

entities.name: Xenares
entities.body: The other, and the one whose party carried the vote that kept the Boeotian alliance when Nicias came to ask for it to be given up.

entities.name: Xenares
entities.body: Cnidis’s son, the Lacedaemonian commanding at Heraclea in Trachis, and among the slain when the neighbouring tribes beat the Heracleots. The history does not say whether he is the ephor.

entities.name: Cnidis
entities.body: Xenares the commander’s father.

entities.name: Eustrophus
entities.body: One of the two Argives sent to Lacedaemon as the men most likely to be acceptable, to get the best treaty they could and be left in peace. They came back with a fifty years’ truce that left the Cynurian land to be settled, if either side chose, by a formal challenge and a battle.

entities.name: Aeson
entities.body: The other of the two.

entities.name: Andromedes
entities.body: One of the three Lacedaemonians sent to take Panactum and the Athenian prisoners from the Boeotians and hand them back. They found Panactum razed, brought the prisoners to Athens, and announced the demolition as though it were as good as restitution.

entities.name: Phaedimus
entities.body: The second of the three.

entities.name: Antimenidas
entities.body: The third.

entities.name: Androsthenes
entities.body: An Arcadian, victor for the first time in the wrestling and boxing at the Olympic games from which Lacedaemon was excluded.

entities.name: Agesippidas
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian whom the Boeotians sent away from Heraclea for misgovernment, having occupied the place themselves; and the commander of the three hundred men slipped into Epidaurus by sea under the Athenians’ noses.

entities.name: Thrasylus
entities.body: One of the five Argive generals, who with Alciphron and on nobody’s authority but their own went out between the armies and got Agis to grant a four-month truce — throwing away the best field Argos would ever have. The Argives began to stone him in the bed of the Charadrus; he reached the altar and saved his life, and lost his property.

entities.name: Alciphron
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian proxenus at Argos, and the other man who went out to parley with Agis.

entities.name: Hipponoidas
entities.body: One of the two polemarchs ordered, in the moment of the onset at Mantinea, to fill the gap Agis had just opened on his own left. He would not move over, and was banished from Sparta afterwards on the charge of cowardice.

entities.name: Aristocles
entities.body: The other polemarch who would not move over, and was banished with him. Not Pleistoanax’s brother.

entities.name: Endius
entities.body: One of the three Lacedaemonians reputed well disposed toward Athens, sent in haste to keep the Argive alliance from being made — and made to look insincere in the assembly by Alcibiades.

entities.name: Leon
entities.body: Another of the three.

entities.name: Heracles
entities.body: By whose temple outside Mantinea the Lacedaemonians camped, and to whose temple they came back from diverting the water on the morning the Argives appeared in front of them in order of battle.

entities.name: The Lepreans
entities.body: Who gave the Eleans half their land for ending a war with the Arcadians, paid the talent to Olympian Zeus until the Attic war gave them an excuse to stop, and appealed to Lacedaemon when Elis used force. Lacedaemon declared them independent and put a garrison in, and Elis went over to Argos.

entities.name: The Parrhasians
entities.body: Subjects of Mantinea, a faction among whom asked Lacedaemon in. Their country was laid waste, the Mantinean fort at Cypsela razed, and they themselves declared independent.

entities.name: The Maenalians
entities.body: Arcadians in the Lacedaemonian line at Mantinea, and whose men the Argives were to give back under the terms Lichas brought.

entities.name: The Sciritae
entities.body: Who in a Lacedaemonian army always hold the left wing to themselves alone; six hundred of them at Mantinea, ordered out of the line to stretch it and broken in the gap that order made.

entities.name: The Neodamodes
entities.body: Enfranchised Helots, settled with Brasidas’s men at Lepreum on the Elean border and drawn up beside them at Mantinea.

entities.name: The Brasideans
entities.body: The Helots who had gone to Thrace with Brasidas, freed by decree and allowed to live where they liked; at Mantinea they stood next to the Sciritae and were broken with them.

entities.name: The Heracleots
entities.body: Of Heraclea in Trachis, harassed from its foundation by every neighbour it threatened, and beaten at last by the Aenianians, Dolopians, Malians and some of the Thessalians.

entities.name: The Aenianians
entities.body: One of the tribes bordering Heraclea that combined to defeat it.

entities.name: The Cleonaeans
entities.body: Argive allies, next to the Orneans in the line at Mantinea, and among the seven hundred dead counted with the Argives.

entities.name: The Orneans
entities.body: The other small Argive ally in that line. Lacedaemon settled the Argive exiles among them, and Argos razed the town.

entities.name: The Dians
entities.body: Of Dium on Athos, who took Thyssus from the Athenian alliance, and who revolted to the Chalcidians themselves two years later.

entities.name: The Patrians
entities.body: Whom Alcibiades induced to carry their walls down to the sea.

entities.name: The Orchomenians
entities.body: Of Orchomenos in Arcadia, where Lacedaemon had lodged her Arcadian hostages. Alarmed by a weak wall and a large army, they joined the league, gave hostages of their own to Mantinea, and gave up the ones they were holding. Not the Boeotians of the same name.

entities.name: Cleomedes
entities.body: Lycomedes’s son, one of the two Athenian generals who camped on Melos and sent envoys in before doing any damage to the land. The Melians would not let them speak before the people.

entities.name: Lycomedes
entities.body: Cleomedes’s father. The history does not say whether he is the Lycomedes whose son Archestratus went to Potidaea.

entities.name: Tisias
entities.body: Tisimachus’s son, the other general at Melos.

entities.name: Tisimachus
entities.body: Tisias’s father.

entities.name: Philocrates
entities.body: Demeas’s son, who brought the reinforcements that pressed the siege of Melos to its end.

entities.name: Demeas
entities.body: Philocrates’s father.

entities.name: Thucles
entities.body: Who brought the first Hellenes to Sicily — Chalcidians out of Euboea — and founded Naxos and the altar of Apollo Archegetes on which the deputies for the games still sacrifice before sailing; and who five years after Syracuse was founded drove the Sicels out and founded Leontini and Catana. Not Eurymedon’s father.

entities.name: Archias
entities.body: One of the Heraclids from Corinth, who founded Syracuse the year after Naxos by driving the Sicels off the island the inner city stands on. Not the Camarinaean who was going to betray his town.

entities.name: Evarchus
entities.body: Whom the Catanians chose as their founder, though Thucles and the Chalcidians settled the place. Not the tyrant of Astacus.

entities.name: Lamis
entities.body: Who brought a colony from Megara, founded Trotilus and then Thapsus, and died before his companions were driven out and given Hyblaean Megara.

entities.name: Hyblon
entities.body: A Sicel king, who gave up the place and invited the Megarians there.

entities.name: Gelo
entities.body: The Syracusan tyrant who expelled the Megarians of Sicily from their city and country after two hundred and forty-five years, and depopulated Camarina.

entities.name: Pamillus
entities.body: Who came from the mother city Megara to help found Selinus.

entities.name: Antiphemus
entities.body: From Rhodes, who with Entimus of Crete led the colony that founded Gela in the forty-fifth year after Syracuse.

entities.name: Entimus
entities.body: From Crete, the other founder of Gela.

entities.name: Aristonous
entities.body: One of the two founders the Geloans gave to Acragas.

entities.name: Pystilus
entities.body: The other founder of Acragas.

entities.name: Perieres
entities.body: From Cuma, one of the two founders of Zancle — which the Sicels named for its shape, zanclon being their word for a sickle.

entities.name: Crataemenes
entities.body: From Chalcis, the other founder of Zancle.

entities.name: Anaxilas
entities.body: Tyrant of Rhegium, who drove out the Samians who had driven out the first settlers of Zancle, peopled the town with a mixed population, and renamed it Messina after his own old country.

entities.name: Euclides
entities.body: One of the three who founded Himera from Zancle, where the language came out a mixture of Chalcidian and Doric and the institutions Chalcidian.

entities.name: Simus
entities.body: The second of the three founders of Himera.

entities.name: Sacon
entities.body: The third.

entities.name: Daxon
entities.body: One of the two Syracusan founders of Camarina.

entities.name: Menecolus
entities.body: The other.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: Tyrant of Gela, who took the land of Camarina in ransom for Syracusan prisoners and resettled the place as its founder. Not Ariphron’s son, and not the Lacedaemonian of Book 8.

entities.name: Italus
entities.body: A king of the Sicels, from whom Italy took its name.

entities.name: Xenophanes
entities.body: Lamachus’s father.

entities.name: The Cyclopes
entities.body: With the Laestrygones, the earliest inhabitants spoken of in any part of Sicily. Thucydides says he cannot tell what race they were, where they came from or where they went, and leaves his readers to the poets.

entities.name: The Laestrygones
entities.body: The other people of that first account, and equally unknown.

entities.name: The Sicanians
entities.body: Who claim to be the first of all and aboriginal, but who the facts show were Iberians driven by the Ligurians from the river Sicanus. They gave the island the name Sicania, were beaten by the Sicels and pushed into the south and west, and hold it still.

entities.name: The Ligurians
entities.body: Who drove the Sicanians out of Iberia.

entities.name: The Iberians
entities.body: What the Sicanians really were; and, Alcibiades told the Lacedaemonians, among the barbarians Athens meant to hire — confessedly the most warlike known.

entities.name: The Elymi
entities.body: Trojans who escaped the Achaeans at the fall of Ilium and settled next to the Sicanians, with some Phocians storm-carried from Troy by way of Libya; their towns are Eryx and Egesta.

entities.name: The Opicans
entities.body: Whom the Sicels were fleeing when they crossed from Italy on rafts, watching for the wind down the strait.

entities.name: The Myletidae
entities.body: Syracusan exiles beaten in a civil war, who joined the Chalcidians in settling Himera.

entities.name: The Egestaeans
entities.body: At war with their Selinuntine neighbours over marriages and a border, and the people who talked Athens into Sicily — reminding her of the alliance made in Laches’s time, warning that Dorians would one day come to the help of Dorians, and promising money. They showed the first Athenian envoys the treasures at the temple of Aphrodite on Eryx, and privately lent one another the same gold and silver plate from banquet to banquet until the sailors went home talking of riches. What could actually be produced was thirty talents.

entities.name: The Selinuntines
entities.body: Who had the Syracusans for allies and were pressing Egesta hard by land and sea, and whose contingent was the strongest of the Syracusan allies in the first battle.

entities.name: The Siceliots
entities.body: Thucydides’s word for the Hellenes settled in Sicily, as against the Sicels and the other barbarians of the island. Hermocrates told them their quarrel was with an appetite, not with a nationality; Alcibiades told Athens they were mixed rabbles with no feeling of patriotism, who would come over one by one as they got a fair offer.

entities.name: The Geloans
entities.body: Who founded Acragas, resettled Camarina for the third time, and sent two hundred horse to the Syracusan line in the first battle.

entities.name: Athenagoras
entities.body: The leader of the people at Syracuse and very powerful with the masses, who answered Hermocrates by saying the reports were concocted by men who wanted the city frightened into their hands; that no shrewd people would start a second war before finishing the first; and that democracy means the whole state while oligarchy means a part. He was wrong about the expedition and, on his own account of the young men of Syracuse, not wrong about much else.

entities.name: Myrrhine
entities.body: Callias’s daughter, by whom Hippias had the five children named on the pillar on the Acropolis — which is part of how Thucydides knows that Hippias, not Hipparchus, was the elder and the tyrant.

entities.name: Callias
entities.body: Hyperechides’s son, and Myrrhine’s father. None of the other three men of the name.

entities.name: Hyperechides
entities.body: Callias’s father.

entities.name: Pisistratus
entities.body: Hippias’s son, named for his grandfather, who held the yearly archonship and dedicated the altar of the twelve gods in the marketplace and the altar of Apollo in the Pythian precinct. The Athenians lengthened the first altar and rubbed out his inscription; the second one is still there in faded letters.

entities.name: Archedice
entities.body: Hippias’s daughter, married off to a Lampsacene because the family had influence with Darius; her tomb at Lampsacus says that pride was never known to her, though she was daughter, wife and sister to the throne.

entities.name: Aeantides
entities.body: Son of the tyrant of Lampsacus, who married Archedice and gave the exiled Hippias his first refuge.

entities.name: Artemis
entities.body: In whose precinct outside Rhegium the armament camped when the town would not let it inside the walls, and where a market was provided for it.

entities.name: Aphrodite
entities.body: To whose temple on Eryx the Egestaeans took the first Athenian envoys, to show them silver plate that gave an impression of wealth quite out of proportion to its value.

entities.name: The Alcmaeonidae
entities.body: The banished family who with the Lacedaemonians put the tyranny down — not, Thucydides insists, Harmodius and the Athenians themselves, which is exactly what the commons had been told.

entities.name: The Thetes
entities.body: The lowest of the Athenian property classes; seven hundred of them were shipped as marines in the first Sicilian armament.

entities.name: The Italiots
entities.body: The Hellenes of Italy, whose decision the Rhegians said they would wait for; the Syracusan envoys tried on their way to Corinth to convince them the expedition threatened Italy as much as Sicily.

entities.name: The Cretans
entities.body: Eighty of the four hundred and eighty archers with the first armament.

entities.name: Heraclides
entities.body: Lysimachus’s son, one of the three generals with full powers elected on Hermocrates’s advice — and elected again, under the same name, when the generals of the investment were deposed and blamed.

entities.name: Lysimachus
entities.body: Heraclides the Syracusan’s father. Not Aristides’s father.

entities.name: Sicanus
entities.body: Execestes’s son, the third of the three Syracusan generals. He shares his name with the river in Iberia the Sicanians were driven from, which carries no card.

entities.name: Execestes
entities.body: Sicanus’s father.

entities.name: Euphemus
entities.body: The Athenian ambassador at Camarina, who answered Hermocrates by conceding everything and claiming it as a right: that fear holds the empire together, that no one can be quarrelled with for providing for his own safety, and that for an imperial city nothing is unreasonable if it is expedient and nobody is a kinsman unless he is sure.

entities.name: Gylippus
entities.body: Cleandridas’s son, named by Lacedaemon to command for the Syracusans on Alcibiades’s advice. Hearing on the way that Syracuse was already invested — which was false — he gave the island up for lost and crossed to Tarentum to save Italy instead, tried to claim at Thurii the citizenship his father had held, was blown out to sea off the Terinaean gulf, and put back to refit. Nicias heard he was coming, counted his four ships, and set the voyage down as piracy.

entities.name: Cleandridas
entities.body: Gylippus’s father, whose citizenship at Thurii his son tried to claim.

entities.name: Diomilus
entities.body: An exile from Andros, given six hundred picked men to hold Epipolae. The Athenians landed at Leon and went up at a run by Euryelus while the Syracusans were still at a review three miles away; he came on in disorder and was killed with about three hundred of them.

entities.name: Pythen
entities.body: The Corinthian who crossed with Gylippus to Tarentum.

entities.name: Eucles
entities.body: One of the three generals elected at Syracuse when the generals of the investment were deposed. Not the Athenian who lost Amphipolis.

entities.name: Tellias
entities.body: The third of them.

entities.name: Phytodorus
entities.body: One of the three commanders of the thirty ships that landed in Laconia itself and so gave Lacedaemon her open pretext. Both editions spell him so, and neither gives him a patronymic or connects him with either Pythodorus.

entities.name: Laespodius
entities.body: The second of the three.

entities.name: Demaratus
entities.body: The third.

entities.name: The Hermae
entities.body: The square stone figures of Hermes that stood in doorways all over Athens, and whose faces were nearly all mutilated in a single night while the expedition was fitting out. Nobody ever found out who did it. The city took it for an omen and for the beginning of a conspiracy against the democracy, offered rewards, invited informers of any status, and executed or outlawed on the word of a prisoner who bought his own impunity — after which, Thucydides says, it was still not clear whether the sufferers had been punished unjustly.

entities.name: The Inessaeans
entities.body: Whose corn the Athenians burnt on the way back to Catana.

entities.name: The Hybleans
entities.body: Whose corn was burnt with it; the Athenians had already failed to storm their town.

entities.name: The Thurians
entities.body: Who would not give Gylippus back his father’s citizenship, and who like Nicias thought four ships could only mean piracy.

entities.name: The Hellespontines
entities.body: Named by Hermocrates with the Ionians and the islanders as peoples who change continually but always serve a master — against free Dorians dwelling in Sicily.
